findings.title: State-mutating HTTP endpoints have no authentication or CSRF/Host protection
findings.description: The Flask app exposes destructive, unauthenticated POST endpoints — /api/restore (overwrites the live save), /api/backup/delete, /api/save/rename, /api/config, and /api/shutdown. There is no CSRF token, no Origin/Referer check, and no Host-header allow-list. Even bound to 127.0.0.1, the server is reachable by any process/page on the machine, and is exposed to two real browser-based attacks while the GUI is running: (1) DNS-rebinding — a malicious site can rebind its hostname to 127.0.0.1 and then issue same-origin requests to port 8080, and (2) cross-origin requests that browsers permit without preflight. Because get_json(silent=True) is used, an attacker doesn't even need a valid JSON content type to reach the handler logic in some configurations. A single forged request to /api/restore can irrecoverably replace the user's current save with an old backup; /api/shutdown can kill the app. The --host option also lets a user trivially bind 0.0.0.0, exposing all of this to the LAN with zero auth.
findings.suggestion: Validate the Host header against an explicit allow-list (127.0.0.1:PORT / localhost:PORT) and reject everything else (blocks DNS-rebinding). Require a Origin/Referer same-origin check on all mutating routes, or issue a per-session CSRF token embedded in PAGE and verified server-side. Generate a random token at startup and require it as a header on /api/* calls. Refuse to bind a non-loopback host unless an explicit --allow-remote flag plus auth is supplied.

findings.title: WatcherManager mutates shared state with no lock under a threaded Flask server
findings.description: Werkzeug's dev server runs with threaded=True by default, so /api/watcher/toggle, /api/watcher/save, /api/restore (pause_for), and /api/save/rename can execute concurrently in different request threads. All of them mutate WatcherManager._watchers, ._watches, ._running, and call self._observer.schedule/unschedule with no synchronization. start() additionally reads-then-rebuilds the observer and re-iterates _watchers while another thread may be inserting into it (RuntimeError: dict changed size during iteration), and watch()/unwatch() race on the same keys. This can corrupt the watch maps, double-schedule observers, or crash a request. The per-watcher SaveWatcher is internally locked, but the manager that owns them is not.
findings.suggestion: Add a threading.Lock (or RLock) to WatcherManager and guard every method that touches _watchers/_watches/_running/_observer. Snapshot collections under the lock before iterating (e.g. list(self._watchers.items())) and never call observer.schedule while holding it if that can deadlock with the observer thread — design the critical sections accordingly.

findings.title: get_manager() lazy singleton has a check-then-act race
findings.description: get_manager() does `if _manager is None: _manager = WatcherManager()` with no lock. Under the threaded Flask server, two concurrent first requests (e.g. index render + an /api/* call) can both observe None and each construct a WatcherManager, each with its own watchdog Observer. One instance is then discarded but may already have been started/scheduled, leaking an observer thread and producing inconsistent watcher state depending on which manager each later request happens to read.
findings.suggestion: Guard initialization with a module-level threading.Lock using double-checked locking, or instantiate the singleton eagerly at import time. Given the manager owns OS threads, a single authoritative instance is important.

findings.title: _do_backup holds the watcher lock across the entire copytree
findings.description: _do_backup acquires self._lock and then calls create_backup(...) — a full shutil.copytree of a PZ save that can be hundreds of MB to gigabytes — while still holding the lock. on_modified(), pause(), cancel_pending(), and resume() all block on the same lock, so the watchdog observer thread (which calls on_modified) is stalled for the entire duration of the copy. This defeats debouncing, lets the watchdog event queue back up, and makes pause_for() during a concurrent restore block until the in-flight backup finishes. The lock should only protect the small bookkeeping (timer, timestamps, ignore window), not the long I/O.
findings.suggestion: Inside the lock, re-check cooldown/mtime and capture the decision + clear the timer; then release the lock and perform create_backup outside it; re-acquire briefly only to append to _backups and update _last_backup_time/_last_backup_mtime. Guard against overlapping backups with a separate 'in progress' flag rather than the bookkeeping lock.

findings.title: /api/config writes arbitrary keys with no allow-list
findings.description: api_config iterates over every key in the posted JSON and calls config_set(key, value) for all of them. There is no allow-list of permitted settings, so a forged or buggy client can pollute config.json with arbitrary keys, and can repoint backups_dir to any path the user can write (e.g. a synced/cloud folder or a location chosen to clobber unrelated files via the game_mode/save_name/timestamp tree). Combined with A1 this is reachable cross-origin.
findings.suggestion: Restrict writes to the known DEFAULTS keys; reject unknown keys with a 400. For backups_dir, validate it is an absolute, writable directory and not a sensitive system path before persisting.

findings.title: Path-component validation is duplicated three ways across modules
findings.description: There are three overlapping validators: saves.get_save() inline check (.., /, \, \x00), saves._validate_name() (adds empty/IP/length/_SANE_NAME_RE), and backup._validate_component() (adds empty/'.'/timestamp). They diverge subtly — e.g. _validate_component rejects '.' and empty while get_save does not, and only _validate_name rejects IP-shaped/over-long names. This is exactly the kind of security boundary where drift causes a bypass, and CLAUDE.md explicitly says to reuse _validate_component. The knowledge is spread across two modules with no single source of truth.
findings.suggestion: Centralize one validate_component(value, label) in a single module (e.g. saves.py) and have backup.py, get_save, and rename paths all call it. Keep the stricter superset (reject '', '.', '..', '/', '\', '\x00', overlong) in one place and unit-test it once.

findings.title: Backups have no completion marker — a crash mid-move leaves a partial backup indistinguishable from a good one
findings.description: create_backup reserves the destination dir, copies into a sibling temp, then moves items into the destination one-by-one. The reserved destination directory exists from the very first mkdir. If the process is killed during the per-item move loop (or during the copytree before it), list_backups() will still enumerate the half-populated destination directory as a valid BackupRecord, and restore_backup will happily restore a truncated save over the live one. The atomicity claim in CLAUDE.md ('atomically move contents') only holds per-file, not for the backup as a whole.
findings.suggestion: Write a completion sentinel (e.g. .pz-complete) as the final step of create_backup, and have list_backups/get_backup ignore (or flag) destinations lacking it. Alternatively build the backup fully in the temp dir and do a single atomic rename of the temp dir onto the final destination, abandoning the move-loop.

findings.title: Configured debounce/cooldown are ignored on the per-save watch path
findings.description: api_watcher_save calls manager.watch(save) with the hardcoded defaults (debounce 5s, cooldown 300s), while api_watcher_toggle passes the configured backup_cooldown_minutes. So whether your cooldown setting is honored depends on which button started watching — 'Watch' on a single save silently ignores the user's configured cooldown and debounce entirely. debounce_seconds from config is never threaded into the watcher at all.
findings.suggestion: Read debounce_seconds and backup_cooldown_minutes from config in a single helper and pass them consistently from both watch entry points (and from auto_start_watcher startup if added).

findings.title: Inconsistent default for backup_cooldown_minutes
findings.description: api_watcher_toggle uses config_get_all().get('backup_cooldown_minutes', 5), but config.DEFAULTS sets backup_cooldown_minutes to 1. The inline fallback of 5 is dead (get_all always fills the default) but signals a stale assumption and would mislead a maintainer about the real default.
findings.suggestion: Drop the redundant inline default and rely on DEFAULTS, or align the literal with DEFAULTS so the intended value is unambiguous.

findings.title: Dead import in gui_command --no-browser branch
findings.description: The --no-browser branch does `import flask` but never uses the module; it then imports app from .gui and calls app.run. The unused import is misleading and duplicates the run logic already in run_gui (which only differs by the webbrowser.open call), so the two startup paths can drift.
findings.suggestion: Remove the unused `import flask`. Refactor run_gui to take an open_browser: bool = True flag and have both CLI branches call it, eliminating the duplicated app.run/print block.

overall_assessment: The core file-system safety work is genuinely good: path-traversal guards, symlink skipping, TOCTOU-safe destination reservation, restore staging with crash recovery, and atomic config writes are all present and backed by adversarial tests. The weak spots are at the boundaries the security tests don't cover: the Flask layer has no auth/CSRF/Host protection over destructive endpoints, and the WatcherManager concurrency model assumes single-threaded access that the default threaded Flask server violates. Validation logic is also duplicated across three functions, which is risky for a security boundary. None of these are catastrophic for a purely single-user loopback desktop tool, but they are real and fixable.
summary: 0 blockers, 4 majors (web auth/CSRF, 3 concurrency in WatcherManager), 4 minors, 2 nits — solid FS safety, but the HTTP and threading boundaries need hardening.
